title: What Cobb learned from Joe Thomas: simplicity
summary: Cobb says he is a simple player influenced by Joe Thomas's simple, effective solos, including a four-note modulation on Cheating on Me.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Now -- yeah, one thing. You know we've mentioned Joe Thomas several times, and you said that (inaudible). Of course, you don't really sound alike in a sense. You both have a lot of drive but --

Stanley, he impressed me from simplicity. And I am a simple player. I don't play a lot of notes. And this is what I mean when he influenced me. Joe couldn't make a modulation (inaudible), say just take a thing. I'm going to give you a situation that he did. If -- you remember the tune, Cheating On Me. And Joe made a modulation on his horn. He played the solo. He said, la-da-doh-dah, da-dah, do-dee, doo-dat, hot-dod, do-da-da-da-da-dee-da-do-dah-yawp, pa-doodle-doo-doo-dah. He said, la-hi-do-dee-do-da, ha-da-da-da-do-do doo-doo-doo-dah, ha . . . and he's in another key, and (inaudible) singing now. You all see what that modulation was? He says, Solomon gave it to him. He said, I didn't know about no modulation. And you take a few notes of modulation and you're in another key.
Bah-dee-do-da-da, that's all it was. And they say, Cheating on me -- oh, that was a bear.

But simplicity's what you got to listen to (inaudible). That's what impressed me about Joe. Everything Joe did was simple but effective. And you can take it today if you simple people go for it. Everybody, all your laymans out here, they don't know nothing about no chord changes.
